title: The ENTIRE History of Ancient Egypt in 10 Minutes
youtube_title: The ENTIRE History of Ancient Egypt in 10 Minutes
description:
From King Narmer uniting two kingdoms around 3100 BC to Cleopatra and the Romans in 30 BC, this is three thousand years of ancient Egypt in about ten minutes: the Great Pyramid and the paid crews who built it, a woman who became pharaoh, a sun-worshipping rebel king, the boy king Tut, the oldest surviving peace treaty and the first recorded strike in history. Every fact is checked, and legends are labelled as legends.

Chapters are added automatically.

#history #ancientegypt #pyramids #cleopatra #animatedhistory

beats.say: November 1922, Egypt's Valley of the Kings. A British archaeologist named Howard Carter is about to peek into a tomb nobody has opened in over three thousand years.
He'd been searching this valley for years, paid for by a rich British lord, Lord Carnarvon, who was running out of patience.
Well, Carter? Can you see anything?
Yes. Wonderful things!
That's how Carter himself remembered the moment.

show.text: Can you see anything? ... Yes, wonderful things.
show.who: Howard Carter, remembering 26 November 1922, in his book The Tomb of Tut.ankh.Amen

beats.say: Gold. Statues. Chariots. More than five thousand objects, packed into the tomb of a teenage king called Tutankhamun.
And Tut wasn't even an important pharaoh. So what was the rest of Egypt like? Let's go back. Five thousand years back.

show.text: The ENTIRE History of Ancient Egypt in 10 Minutes

beats.say: Egypt is basically a long green stripe of farmland along the Nile river, with desert on both sides.
Every summer the Nile flooded and left rich black mud behind. Free fertilizer, every single year. That's why people settled there.
Confusingly, the south was called Upper Egypt and the north Lower Egypt, because the Nile flows north. Upstream is up.
Around 3100 BC, a king named Narmer united the two lands into one kingdom.
One Egypt. Two crowns. Both mine.
Lovely. I'll write that down. We only just invented writing.
Hieroglyphs were little pictures that could stand for sounds or for whole ideas. Some of the oldest ones come from right around this time.
A carved stone called the Narmer Palette shows him wearing the white crown of the south on one side, and the red crown of the north on the other.
Egypt's kings were later called pharaohs, and people believed they were gods on Earth. Great way to win every argument.
About five hundred years later, a pharaoh named Khufu built the biggest tomb in history: the Great Pyramid of Giza.
Why build a mountain? Pyramids were royal tombs. Egyptians believed the king lived on after death, so he needed a safe and spectacular home forever.
That's also why they made mummies. They dried and wrapped bodies, so the dead would still have a body in the afterlife.
It's made of about two point three million stone blocks, and the average block weighs more than a car.

show.label: Stone blocks in the Great Pyramid
show.sub: the average one is heavier than a car

beats.say: It stood about a hundred and forty-seven metres tall. Nothing people built was taller for about three thousand eight hundred years, until an English cathedral spire around 1311.
And who built it? Not slaves, like old movies show.
Archaeologists found the workers' town next door, with bakeries, and a cemetery where workers were buried near the pyramids. Slaves didn't get that honour.
Pay day! What is it this time?
Bread and beer. Same as yesterday. You're welcome.
The crews even had team names, painted on the stones. Archaeologists found gangs called Friends of Khufu, and Drunkards of Menkaure.
Later, a pharaoh called Pepi the Second became king at about six years old, and ruled for over sixty years. Maybe even ninety.
You might have heard he smeared servants with honey, so flies would bite them instead of him. No Egyptian record says that. It's a legend.
After Pepi, the kingdom fell apart for a while. That kept happening in Egypt: it would split up, then come back together, stronger.
Jump ahead to the New Kingdom, Egypt's richest era. In 1479 BC, a little boy became king, and his aunt and stepmother Hatshepsut ruled for him.
By now, kings weren't building pyramids anymore. They were buried in hidden tombs in the Valley of the Kings, so robbers couldn't find them. Spoiler: robbers found almost all of them.
Within a few years, she simply made herself pharaoh.
But Your Majesty, pharaohs have beards.
Then fetch me a beard.
Her statues really do show her with the pharaoh's fake ceremonial beard. Male pharaohs wore fake ones too.
She ruled for about twenty years and sent ships to a faraway land called Punt, which came back loaded with incense trees and exotic animals.
But after she died, her stepson Thutmose the Third had many of her statues smashed and her name scratched off. Historians still debate why.

show.title: The Sun King and the Boy King

beats.say: Around 1350 BC came Akhenaten, a pharaoh who did something shocking. He told Egypt to worship one god above all: the sun disc, called the Aten.
He shut the temples of the old gods and built a brand new capital city in the desert.
You closed our temples?
Relax. The sun is all you need. It's literally right there.
It didn't last. Soon after, a boy of about nine became king: Tutankhamun.
His advisers brought back the old gods and abandoned Akhenaten's city. Then Tut died young, and historians still argue about what killed him.
He was only about nineteen.

show.label: Tutankhamun's age when he died
show.sub: about 19, after roughly ten years as king

beats.say: His small tomb was later buried under rubble and forgotten. That's why it was still packed with treasure in 1922.
The most famous pharaoh of all was Ramesses the Second, who ruled for about sixty-six years.
He put giant statues of himself all over Egypt, including four enormous ones at a temple called Abu Simbel. By some counts, he also had about a hundred children.
In 1274 BC, he marched north to fight the Hittites, a powerful empire from what's now Turkey, at a city called Kadesh, in modern Syria.
It was one of the biggest chariot battles ever, with thousands of chariots. And Ramesses walked straight into a trap.
He fought his way out, but neither side really won. So naturally, both sides went home and said they'd won.
Carve it on every temple. I won!
Funny. We're writing that we won.
About fifteen years later, the two empires made peace. It's the oldest peace treaty in the world that still survives, and a copy hangs at the United Nations.
Now meet the people who dug and painted the royal tombs. They lived in a village called Deir el-Medina, near the Valley of the Kings.
Their pay was grain. So when the grain rations came late under Ramesses the Third, no pay meant no food.
We are hungry! Eighteen days of this month have passed!
Then we stop working. Put the tools down.
They marched past the guard posts and sat down behind a royal temple. It's the first recorded labour strike in history.
Amennakhte wrote it all down on a papyrus that's now in a museum in Turin, Italy. And yes, they eventually got their grain.
After that, Egypt slowly weakened. Over the next centuries, Libyans, Nubians, Assyrians and Persians all took turns ruling it.
In 332 BC, Alexander the Great, a young king from Macedonia in northern Greece, took Egypt almost without a fight.
He founded a city on the coast and named it after himself: Alexandria. Very humble.
After he died, his general Ptolemy grabbed Egypt. Ptolemy's family ruled for almost three hundred years, speaking Greek the whole time.
The last of them was Cleopatra. She was Macedonian Greek, but the Greek writer Plutarch says she was the first of her family to learn Egyptian.
Also in Cleopatra's lifetime, a Greek historian named Diodorus visited Egypt, where cats were sacred. He says he saw an angry crowd kill a Roman visitor who had killed a cat by accident.
She teamed up with Rome's most powerful man, Julius Caesar, and later with the Roman general Mark Antony.
But in 31 BC, Caesar's adopted son Octavian beat Antony and Cleopatra's fleet at the sea battle of Actium.
A year later, with Roman armies closing in, Antony and Cleopatra both took their own lives.
In 30 BC, Egypt became a province of the Roman Empire. Three thousand years of pharaohs, over.
That's so long ago that Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.

show.sub: Cleopatra to the Moon landing: about 2,000

beats.say: After Rome, people slowly forgot how to read hieroglyphs. Meanwhile, for centuries, Europeans ground up mummies and sold the powder as medicine. Really.
Then in 1799, French soldiers found the Rosetta Stone, with the same text in Greek and in Egyptian. In 1822, a Frenchman named Champollion finally cracked hieroglyphs.
A hundred years later, Howard Carter peeked into Tut's tomb, and the whole world went Egypt-crazy all over again.
From Narmer to Cleopatra, that's three thousand years of history. Not bad for a stripe of mud along a river.
